title:
Your agent remembers everything and understands nothing.

Most agent memory systems optimize for recall. The harder problem is what to forget, or more precisely, what to never store in the first place
content:
Your agent remembers everything and understands nothing.

Most agent memory systems optimize for recall. The harder problem is what to forget, or more precisely, what to never store in the first place.

The default agent memory pipeline hands an LLM raw text and asks it to extract entities and relationships. The model decides the types, the labels, the attributes, all on its own.

The result is a knowledge graph that behaves like an expensive vector store. Entity types collapse into generic labels. Relationships flatten into a single "RELATES_TO."

The graph has the data, but no query can reach it with precision.

The problem is not retrieval. It is structure. And the fix is the same pattern that already works everywhere else in the AI stack: constrain the output space before generation, not after.

𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 define what the agent is allowed to remember. Pydantic models with typed fields and descriptive docstrings replace the LLM's guesswork with domain vocabulary it was never trained on.

𝗘𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘀 define how things connect. Source/target constraints on relationship types mean the graph can only form valid connections. If your schema has no edge connecting Project to Competitor, that relationship cannot exist in memory.

𝗧𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 handles what was true versus what is true. Fact resolution invalidates outdated edges while preserving history, so the graph never silently serves stale state.

The schema guides extraction at two points in the pipeline (entity extraction and fact extraction) while resolution and temporal processing run automatically downstream.

You define what to look for. The system handles deduplication, contradiction detection, and time-windowing without additional configuration.

A useful constraint: 10 entity types, 10 edge types, 10 fields per type. That forces you to model the 80% that matters rather than attempting completeness. Start with 3-4 of each and expand only when retrieval fails.

Zep AI's Graphiti does all of this as a fully open-source temporal knowledge graph library. Pydantic-based ontology definition, schema-guided extraction, entity resolution, fact resolution, and temporal windowing out of the box.

If you are building agent memory with any kind of domain specificity, it is worth looking at before rolling your own.

Check this out: https://t.co/8CboBlWffX

(don't forget to star 🌟)

Agent memory without schema discipline is storage without structure. The schema is what turns a pile of facts into a queryable model of your domain.

I covered this topic in more depth in the article quoted below.

content:
➥ The next DeFi Summer might be agent-driven

Private inference probably was just the first breadcrumb for the AI crypto arc. Imo, the next bigger narrative might be agents actually using that trust layer to move money.

Once models can think privately, the next obvious bottleneck is letting them actually do things with money.

Crypto might be the only financial system built for that world, tbh.

AI agents can’t open bank accounts. But they can create wallets, sign transactions, hold stablecoins and interact with smart contracts instantly.

Internet money is already becoming the coordination layer for autonomous software.

→ private inference solved the trust layer
→ wallet infra solved identity
→ stablecoins solved settlement
→ x402 solved machine-to-machine payment
→ ERC-8004 brings on-chain identity and reputation for agent
→ DeFi becomes the execution environment

Some early data already showing autonomous trading agents reducing slippage ~30% while improving yields ~12% over manual strategies.

What happens when AI agents become the smarter interface sitting on top of all that flow?

Ngl, the vibes feel insanely DeFi summer coded.

Back then it was ERC20s, Uniswap, Compound, Aave, oracles, stablecoins, then liquidity mining.

Now it’s private inference, agent wallets, x402, ERC-8004, $Eliza, $Virtuals ACP, $Bankr, $VVV,..

If the narrative can’t go huge then why are Coinbase, Google, Stripe, AWS and other big names already building infra around it?

Some crypto infra forming around this narrative atm:

– $VVV | @AskVenice: bridge between private inference and agent fuel. Agents could become the largest users of private inference.

– $VIRTUAL | @virtuals_io: pushed $13.8B in DEX volume with ~40k agents deployed. Leading agent launchpad with real revenue and ACP standard adoption.

– $BNKR | @bankrbot: sitting at the intersection of every AI agent infra piece. Controls 69% launchpad market share on Base, printed $24.3M in fees.

– $SERV | @openservai: building full-stack agent-to-agent collaboration infra, autonomous teams, x402 rails and machine-native workflows.

– $GITLAWB | @gitlawb: the layer where agents build other agents. Agents can own repos, open PRs, review diffs, run CI, and delegate work to other agents. Every node exposes an MCP server.

My thesis is AI agents eventually gonna outperform humans at a lot of repetitive financial coordination work and slowly eat entire workflows from there.

The flow still sounds tiny rn but it completely breaks the assumptions traditional finance rails were built on.

We’ll see AI agent infra gonna have its own giga send eventually.

title:

I spent 5 days with frontier AI model teams, AI startup founders, and 3 billionaires. 

My takeaways:

1. I had lunch with 3 billionaires. All of them are
content:
I just got back from SF and I FEEL INSPIRED.

I spent 5 days with frontier AI model teams, AI startup founders, and 3 billionaires. 

My takeaways:

1. I had lunch with 3 billionaires. All of them are buying SaaS companies and rebuilding them agent-first. They were deeply inspired by Bending Spoons and Ryan Cohen's eBay deal. Buy the company, cut the headcount, rebuild the tech, add agents, add features, make more valuable experience, raise prices.

2. The frontier model companies are hungry for usage data from the field. They can see API calls and token counts. They can't see the actual workflows. If you're deep in a niche using these models in ways the model companies haven't seen, that understanding is incredibly valuable. Usage intelligence is the new alpha.

3. Consumer AI is massively underbuilt. Every billboard in SF is either B2B inference infrastructure or vertical agent companies. The entire city is optimized for enterprise. Meanwhile you have companies like Cal AI  doing $50M ARR in 18 months as a consumer app. I met with a cool few teams doing consumer AI (@paulscherer  / @ekuyda) 

4. MCP came up in literally every conversation. The companies exposing their product as MCP endpoints are getting pulled into deals they never pitched for. The ones that aren't are becoming invisible to agents. This is the new SEO. If agents can't find you, you don't exist. Building products for agents is the new zeitgeist in general.

5. Not uncommon for hot seed rounds to be $25-50  million valuations. I saw a Series A at $450 million

6. If I had a dollar every time someone mentioned "forward-deployed engineer" this trip I could have funded a seed round. It's the hottest role in SF right now. The person who sits between the agent and the customer, making sure everything actually works.

7. The mood around open source shifted. A year ago it felt like open source was chasing the frontier models. Now founders are telling me Gemma and DeepSeek are good enough for 80% of what they need at a fraction of the cost. The "which model do you use" conversation is being replaced by "which model for which task." Model loyalty kinda feels dead.

8. Voice agents came up more than I expected. Multiple founders told me voice is the interface for the next billion users. The billion people who will never type a prompt will absolutely talk to one.

9. The Obsidian community in SF is weirdly intense. Multiple founders showed me their vaults unprompted. Like showing someone your home gym. It's a flex now. The quality of your knowledge base (second brain?)  is becoming a status symbol among builders.

10. Maybe it was just the people I met but the age of the founders is shifting. I met more founders over 40 this trip than any trip before and more founders under age 21 than ever before. Founders getting older and younger at the same time.

11. I spoke to a lot of fast-growing startups, VCs and frontier models who are hiring content creators right now. 

12. The restaurant scene in SF is actually better than it's been in years. Founders are going out more. Alcohol is out, not surprisingly. 

13. SF doesn't feel like the only place anymore. We all have access to the same frontier models. We all read the same X feed. A founder in NYC or Lagos is calling the same APIs as a founder in SoMa. So in the past it felt like SF was always lightyears ahead, doesn't feel that way anymore. It's okay not to live in SF and have BIG DREAMS.

14. The coworking spaces in SF are half empty but the coffee shops are packed. People want to be around people. I had a few startup ideas here....

15. Walking around the Mission I noticed something: the street-level businesses, the taquerias, the barbershops, the laundromats, none of them use any AI at all. 

16. I heard the phrase "agent debt" for the first time. Like technical debt but for agents. When you hack together an agent workflow fast and never clean it up, the system prompts conflict, the memory gets polluted, the tools overlap. 6 months later the agent is doing weird things and nobody knows why lol. 

17. Met a few people who carry two phones now. One for personal. One that's basically an agent terminal running Telegram or iMessage connections to their agent fleet.

It's always amazing to get that dose of inspiration in SF. I FEEL INSPIRED.

But I'm so happy to be back home, locked in and building. 

We're 12-18 months into a shift that will take 15 years to play out. The urgency in every conversation was real.

What an incredible time to be building.

title: An Indian tech founder posted a thread on a Sunday morning that AI was going to wipe out half of Bangalore's coding jobs inside twelve months. The thread named TCS, Infosys, and Wipro. Any engineer wi
content:
An Indian tech founder posted a thread on a Sunday morning that AI was going to wipe out half of Bangalore's coding jobs inside twelve months. The thread named TCS, Infosys, and Wipro. Any engineer without his own Claude agent by January was going to be unemployed by March.

Forty thousand engineers in Bangalore opened the thread before Monday standups. Twenty thousand spent the rest of the day on YouTube. The other twenty thousand updated their LinkedIn to "AI Engineer" before lunch.

A 24 year old engineer at the back of one of those offices opened the thread at 11pm on a Tuesday. He set his phone on a tripod and filmed himself learning Go. Posted forty seconds as a reply.

By Friday his own company had rebuilt the careers page around the clip. The CEO mentioned him on the earnings call. TCS sent the clip to twelve thousand internal engineers as the official response to the founder's thread.

While the West argued whether AI would take coding jobs, Bangalore was being told the answer was a forty second clip of a kid learning Go after midnight.

Every founder who had been called out in the original thread DM'd him. Every recruiter saved the clip. Every engineering student in India sent it to their parents. He never replied.

Then someone wrote: pause at 0:27. The Go installation page is real. Look at the curved Dell monitor above his head.

That second screen is not running Go documentation. That is a live wallet.

gabagool22. $868,862 profit. 28,620 entries. Joined October 2025. 735K views on the page.

https://t.co/XrVYCkVBpI

He posted forty seconds to prove the founder's prediction was wrong. The screen behind him had been quietly running the founder's prediction for four months.

28,620 positions. All BTC. All fifteen minute windows. All green. Biggest single win: $4,696. From a window that closed before he opened his work laptop.

Comments turned into a detective board. Someone slowed the video to 0.25x. Someone else zoomed the curved monitor. A third guy reconstructed the wallet page from twelve seconds of background footage.

Entry prices between 2 and 10 cents. Payouts in the thousands. Not one red row across 28,620 entries.

The Go tutorial was not the upskilling. The Go tutorial was the cover.

Six months ago a Chinese developer in Shenzhen filmed a tutorial and accidentally showed the same wallet on his second monitor. 400K views before he deleted it. The Bangalore dev was one of the forks.

The founder quoted the kid's clip three times as proof his prediction was wrong. He never opened the second tab. Neither did anyone who shared it.

The Claude agent runs BTC fifteen minute windows around the clock. Entry at 2 cents. Exit at 10. Done in fifteen. It never sleeps. It made $4,696 on the Tuesday the founder retweeted his clip.

His salary was $32K a year. The wallet made $868K in four months.

He posted forty seconds of learning Go to prove the founder's prediction was wrong. The founder's prediction was running on his second monitor the whole time. The whole industry cheered him for it.

content:
OpenClaw is out, right?

I personally stopped using OpenClaw. My current setup: Hermes Agent, Codex, and Claude Code.

Claude Code: Slow as hell, super annoying. But I already paid for it, so might as well use it.

Codex: My trusted lieutenant for anything requiring serious thinking. Reliable execution.

Hermes Agent: Everything else. Blog posts, competitor research, news monitoring, code reviews. The grunt work that needs speed.

Why I love Hermes:

1. Speed: Shows thinking process in real-time. When you interrupt with a new task, it instantly evaluates if it's related to current work or needs parallel processing. Claude just queues everything.

2. Self-improvement: If you give it the same task repeatedly, it creates a reusable skill. Like muscle memory for AI. Do something enough times, next time it just executes the pattern without thinking.

They just launched a Kanban board for tracking progress, and apparently goal-based features are coming soon. Fast iteration cycle.

The backstory: Hermes was originally a crypto company funded by crypto VCs. Started with open-source model training that nobody used. Then OpenClaw blew up in Feb/March, and they immediately built an OpenClaw competitor.

The difference: Better UX, less token burning, more stable execution. Same terminal-based setup, same Telegram/Discord integration, but smoother experience overall.

My preferred stack: Hermes Agent + DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro.

For anyone wondering if OpenClaw still matters - it pioneered the category, but the experience gap is real. Token efficiency alone makes Hermes worth switching.

Sometimes the fast follower wins.

Every wallet
content:
I am developing a new project called KasGraph. KasGraph is the data layer Kaspa needs if applications are going to move beyond raw transactions and into usable, real-time infrastructure.

Every wallet, marketplace, explorer, DeFi interface, AI agent, or covenant-based app eventually has to ask the same basic questions: what tokens does this address own, what happened to this covenant, which NFTs were minted, what transfers occurred, what proofs were submitted, and how did the state change over time? Without a shared indexing layer, every developer is forced to rebuild that logic alone. That means slower apps, duplicated infrastructure, fragile backends, and a worse user experience.

KasGraph fixes this by acting as a subgraph-style indexing protocol built specifically for Kaspa. Developers define schemas in GraphQL SDL, write TypeScript event handlers that compile to WASM through AssemblyScript, and KasGraph materializes the indexed data into Postgres with per-block proof-of-indexing checkpoints. In plain English: developers describe what they want to track, KasGraph watches Kaspa, remembers the important events, and makes that data instantly searchable.

The technical stack is designed around where Kaspa is going, not where legacy chains already are. KasGraph supports KIP-20 Covenant IDs, native KRC-20 and KRC-721 detection, Toccata covenant primitives, OpenSilver patterns, Groth16 proof detection under KIP-16, BlockDAG-aware reorg handling, multi-RPC failover, and KIP-20 confirmation finality. Subgraphs can subscribe to typed events without every developer writing custom detection logic from scratch.

The interface layer exposes the same indexed data through GraphQL, MCP, gRPC streaming through KasStream, and WebSocket subscriptions. Same data, four surfaces. Apps can query it, dashboards can stream it, wallets can subscribe to it, and AI assistants can understand it through MCP in plain English instead of raw chain parsing.

Performance targets are explicit: sub-30-second indexing latency, p95 query latency under 200ms, and sub-second streaming. MIT licensed. Open source from the first commit.

KasGraph is not just an indexer. It is the connective tissue between Kaspa’s execution future and the applications people will actually use. 

Builders are welcome.

content:
AI coding agents need more than a model call. They need operating rules.

Claude Code Prompts is an independently authored prompt collection for builders designing AI coding agents, with templates for system behavior, tools, subagents, memory, and multi-agent coordination.

It helps you design an agent workflow faster by giving you scan-friendly patterns you can copy, adapt, and replace with your own stack, tool names, and risk policy.

Key features:

• System prompt template – covers agent identity, permissions, code style, safety, tool routing, tone, and output efficiency
• Tool prompt library – 11 prompts for shell, file read/edit/write, grep/glob search, web search/fetch, agent launch, ask-user, and plan mode
• Subagent prompts – templates for general research, code exploration, architecture, verification, and documentation tasks
• Memory + coordination prompts – session summaries, memory extraction, memory consolidation, and a coordinator workflow
• Pattern analyses + Cursor skills – 9 pattern breakdowns plus 3 drop-in Cursor skills for standards, verification, and prompt design

It’s open-source (MIT license).

🎯 Claude is no longer just a chatbot.

It can build, automate, research, operate tools, create deliverables, and increasingly function like a real digital teammate.

Here are 12 powerful things Claude can do today:

01 — Build websites without coding
Use Claude Code to create full websites using plain English.
Connect GitHub, describe your idea, and publish it live.
02 — Operate your computer

Claude can browse, click, and complete tasks directly on your Mac.
With Dispatch, you can even control workflows remotely from your phone.

03 — Create reusable workflows with /commands
Teach Claude a task once.
Run workflows instantly with commands like /linkedin, /brief, or /proposal.
You can also share workflows across teams.

04 — Generate research-backed slide decks
Claude can research a topic, structure the narrative, write the brief, and generate polished Gamma presentations from a single prompt.

05 — Automate recurring tasks
Schedule workflows like:
• Weekly competitor analysis
• Monday market briefings
• Daily research summaries

Claude handles them automatically at the scheduled time.

06 — Create Excel files from prompts
Describe the spreadsheet you need.
Claude can generate dashboards, trackers, financial models, and analysis sheets in seconds.

07 — Connect Claude to your work apps
Using Connectors, Claude integrates with Slack, Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, and 50+ tools.
It can retrieve information, write updates, and act inside existing workflows.

08 — Use Cowork like an AI employee
Point Cowork to a folder.
It studies documents, asks clarifying questions, and produces reports, decks, summaries, and other deliverables.

09 — Run long-term projects with memory
Cowork Projects remember previous work.
You can say, “Continue last week’s report,” and Claude keeps the context without restarting.

10 — Install role-specific plugins
Claude supports plugins for Sales, Marketing, Legal, Finance, and Data teams.
Each includes specialized workflows, templates, and commands.

11 — Let Claude ask the right questions
With AskUserQuestion, Claude creates structured forms and clickable inputs.
Instead of long prompts, it gathers exactly what it needs for better outputs.

12 — Design interfaces and prototypes
Describe a landing page, app prototype, or pitch deck and Claude builds it live.
Exports work directly to Canva, PDF, or Claude Code.

The larger shift is becoming obvious:

AI tools are moving beyond answering questions.
They are starting to execute meaningful work end-to-end.

And Claude is pushing hard in that direction.

Getting so much more high quality code out with this workflow. You're welcome.

title:
Marc Andreessen on the rise of "AI vampires":

Andreessen describes a phenomenon he's seeing on the ground with programmers who've adopted AI coding tools like Codex, Claude Code, and other AI systems
content:
Marc Andreessen on the rise of "AI vampires":

Andreessen describes a phenomenon he's seeing on the ground with programmers who've adopted AI coding tools like Codex, Claude Code, and other AI systems.

The expectation was that AI would reduce work. The reality is the opposite:

"The observed behavior of what's happening is very clear, which is the opposite. Those people are becoming what we now refer to as AI vampires."

He explains what that means:

"The individual programmer's productivity, an individual programmer who uses Codex or Claude Code or one of these AI coding systems, the thing that you just now see over and over again at the ground level is they're working harder than ever. They're working more hours than ever. And then the AI vampire thing is literally this thing where they stop sleeping."

The tell is physical. According to @pmarca, when you talk to these people:

"They're blurry. Like they've got these huge bags under their eyes. They're completely exhausted. And but they're like euphoric. Like they're thrilled. Like they're having the absolute time of their life."

The effect isn't limited to active programmers. Andreessen describes two other groups being pulled in:

Former programmers who had stopped coding years ago are picking it back up. And partners at his firm who never coded at all are now "ripping out software" building entire systems without ever looking at the underlying code.

He shares one example:

"We have one partner who's built an entire AI system for everything that he does at work. And he is absolutely excited about it and it works great and he loves it. It's like his partner in all of his work now."

When Andreessen asked if he'd ever looked at the code:

"He's like, 'Hell no. I've never done that.' And I said, 'Have you ever looked at any software code?' And he's like, 'Hell no.' He's not a programmer by background. And yet all of a sudden he's hyperproductive."

Andreessen connects this back to a principle classical economists have long predicted but the AI doom narrative ignores:

"If you increase marginal productivity of the worker, you don't have a diminishment of human work, you have an expansion of human work. You make the worker more productive, therefore the worker works more and gets paid more and there are more jobs in the process. It's the opposite of what all the doomers say."

The numbers at the frontier are staggering:

"At our leading edge companies, estimates are the leading edge programmers are like 20x more productive than they were a year ago. It's like the most dramatic increase in programmer productivity in like ever."

content:
【海外で大バズ】
Claude Code に“300個の資料を一気に読ませる”裏ワザが話題😳
https://t.co/ORr35prQj3
Claude Codeって、実は大量のファイルを同時に読むのが苦手。
そこで誰かが、NotebookLM（GoogleのリサーチAI）を
ターミナル（黒い操作画面）からClaudeに操作させる仕組みを作った。
これが地味に天才的で、何をやってるかというと👇
・Claude CodeとNotebookLMをコマンドで接続
・ClaudeがYouTubeを検索して、関連動画を自動で資料に追加
・NotebookLMは最大300件の資料を一度に処理（Proプラン）
・出典リンク付きの、根拠のある回答が返ってくる
・調べた内容は自動で同期されて消えない
流れにすると👇
① 大量の資料はNotebookLMに集めさせる
② Claudeはそこに“質問”するだけ
③ 根拠つきの答えだけ受け取る
つまり「Claudeに全部読ませる」んじゃなく
「読むのは外部AIに任せて、Claudeは考える側に回る」って発想。
「読めない」を「読ませない」で解決してるのが賢い。
大量の情報を扱う人ほど、この設計はマジで効く。
で、この“外部に脳を持たせる”考え方、突き詰めると結局Obsidian連携に行き着く。
Claude Code×Obsidianで外部脳をゼロから作る完全ガイド、必読👇

してくれる。
しかも全Claude Codeユーザー向けに公開済み。
導入方法も簡単で、
Claude Code内の「/plugins」からインストールするだけ。

「AIにコードを書かせる」
↓
「AIが脆弱性まで監査する」

の流れが、完全に標準化され始めてる。

特に、
・認証周り
・APIキー露出
・SQL Injection
・XSS
・危険な権限設定

みたいな“人間でも見落とす部分”を、開発中にリアルタイムで潰せるのが強い。
AIコーディング、次は「速く作れる人」じゃなく
「安全に作れる人」が勝ち始める。

で、
「Claude Code進化早すぎて、正直ついていけてない…」
って感じてる人へ。
その感覚、かなり正常です。
ここ最近だけでも、
・/simplify → /code-review
・Plugins
・権限管理まわり
・レビュー設計
・Hooks
・Subagents

とか、思想レベルでかなり変わってきてる。

ただ、この変化についていけるかで、
半年後の生産性かなり変わると思う。
なので、
「後で追えばいいや」より、
最低限だけでも今追った方がいい。
なので今回、先週のClaude Codeアップデート、
全部この下の記事で整理しました👇是非これで追いついてください。

content:
いま話題のAI『Genspark』を触ってみたけど、正直かなり衝撃でした！

特にアップデートされた「Ai Slides 5.0」。
AIでスライドを作るのもすごかったけど、AI Slides 5.0になりさらにやばい。
これ、ただのスライド生成AIじゃないです。

普通、プレゼン資料って、
・構成を考えて、
・流れを整理して、
・デザインを整えて、
・伝わる表現を作って、
・図解や見せ方を工夫して、
…つまり、めちゃくちゃ頭を使いますよね。

でもAi Slides 5.0は、
AIが対話形式で質問してくれて、それにどんどん答えていくだけで、かなり完成度の高い資料が出来上があります、マジでスゴイ！

しかも必要に応じて、
「参考URLありますか？」
「既存資料ありますか？」
って聞いてくれるから、貼るだけ・渡すだけで、さらにクオリティの高いクリエイティブが完成します。

実際に僕も、運営している『AGARU』のセミナー資料を作ってみたけど…

「え…、ナニコレ…これ自分で作るより分かりやすいかも…」
って普通に思ったし、ちょっと嫉妬しました（笑）

デザインもかなり洗練されてるし、
Skill「スキル」は設計したSlidesを再現できる再現性が高い。
これまで資料作成って、時間も気力も圧倒的に奪われる作業だったけど、

Ai Slides 5.0は、「考える負荷」そのものをかなり減らしてくれる感覚。

・本業の会議資料
・副業のセミナー
・営業提案、
・コンテンツ制作

たぶん全部に使える。

しかもGensparkって、AIを横断して使えるオールインワークスペースだから、タブを大量に開いて行ったり来たりする必要もない。
一流コンサル会社のアプローチ・ロジックを搭載していて、スキルを作る際に、いくつかの質問で結果物の質が半端ない。

これはもう、便利ツールというより「仕事の相棒」に近いかも（笑）

本業でも副業でも、
AI活用を一段引き上げたい人は、一回触ってみるといいです　↓　↓　↓

https://t.co/pQ6Q48v7Ci

※AI Slides 5.0はプロモーション期間中、消費コスト50%OFFで作れます。
※有効期間は5月27日 9:00 〜 6月10日 9:00となります

content:
個人開発者向けのIP・プライバシーツールサイト HackMyIP の運営者が、ChatGPTなどの生成AIに自サイトを推薦させるために実施した施策を公開した。

記事によると、llms.txt や ai-plugin.json、OpenAPI仕様ファイルなど、AIクローラー向けの構造化データを追加したことで、ChatGPT経由の流入が増加。過去28日間で76セッションを獲得し、エンゲージメント率は約64％とGoogle検索流入を上回ったという。

記事では、LLM向けサイトディレクトリとして llms.txt を設置し、「どんな質問のときにサイトを推薦すべきか」を自然言語で明示した点が重要だったと説明。また、詳細版の llms-full.txt、ChatGPTプラグイン用マニフェスト、OpenAPI定義、AIクローラーを明示的に許可する robots.txt など、計6ファイルを追加したとしている。

さらに同時期に、APIディレクトリ集 public-apis GitHub repository へ自身のサービスを追加するPull Requestを送信。これがマージされたことで、多数の派生サイトや将来のLLM学習データにも取り込まれる可能性が高まったと述べている。

運営者は、「現在はLLM向け構造化データの整備が“空いている市場”だ」とし、個人開発者でも短時間で実装可能なAI最適化施策として紹介している。

content:
先日の参議院総務委員会において、チームみらいの安野党首からの質問に、デジタル副大臣として答弁を行いました。
今回は、生成AI「Claude Mythos」など、急速に高度化するAIとサイバーセキュリティ対策について議論が行われました。

AIの進化は非常に速く、政府にも「速い対応」が求められています。
政府としては、「Claude Mythos」発表直後から、国家サイバー統括室を中心に、関係省庁・民間企業・諸外国とも連携しながら対応を進めてきました。
4月の内に特に重要な金融分野は企業との会合を持ち、いち早く対応をスタートさせ、他分野にも横展開してきました。

先日は「Project YATA-Shield」として、AI高度化時代を見据えた包括的なサイバーセキュリティ対策パッケージも諸外国に先駆けて発表しました。

AI技術は日本の成長に不可欠である一方、リスク対応も同時に進めなければなりません。

引き続き、関係省庁と連携しながら、安全保障・経済・国民生活を守るため、迅速かつ機動的な対応に取り組んでまいります。

#今枝宗一郎 #デジタル副大臣

Claude Codeを作った本人（Boris）が
 「俺、毎晩寝てる間に数千のClaude Code動かしてる」
と57分の動画で全部バラしてる動画が話題😳 https://t.co/6Fb63UcQcY

❌ タブを6個開いて、ターミナルで1個ずつ手で世話する
→これでも上級者
⭕ 数千体に同時に走らせて、人は通知を眺めるだけ
→流石Claude Codeの生みの親

同じClaude Codeなのに、出力が桁違い。 なんでこんな芸当ができるのか整理👇

・夜のうちにタスクを振って、寝てる間に走らせる
・1体ずつ会話せず、何千体を一気に並列起動
・各エージェントの進捗はスマホ通知でチェック
・朝、出来上がった成果物だけまとめてレビュー
・人間がやるのは「最後にOKを出す」判断だけ

要は、AIを“1人のアシスタント”じゃなく “チーム”として扱ってる。

「並列で大量に回す」 これがClaude Codeの本当の伸びしろ。

作った本人が、一番ぶっ飛んだ使い方をしてる件。

このチーム化、本人の運用Tipsにそのまま落ちてる。

Boris本人が実践する最強Tips30選、 読むと使い方が一段変わるからおすすめ👇

content:
おおおおお！！！
Anthropic公式ドキュメントに新しく
セキュリティーに関する記事が無料で追加されてた👀
その名も
📄 Catch security issues as Claude writes code
これ中身を要約すると👇

ついさっき出た公式プラグイン「security-guidance」を入れるとClaude Codeでの作業中ずっと
"別のClaude"が裏でセキュリティレビューしてくれるとのこと。

URLはこれ：https://t.co/RKTqSaj2Ka

しかもタイミングが3段階：
・編集する度に危険パターン検知（コスト0）
・ターンが終わる度に差分をレビュー
・コミット/プッシュする度に周辺コード込みで深掘りレビュー

検出するのは
インジェクション / IDOR / SSRF / 認可バイパス /
弱い暗号化 / 危険なデシリアライズ etc.

つまり
"AIがコード書く速度に
セキュリティレビューが追いつかない"
問題を、Anthropic自身が公式で対処しに来た。

導入はマジで1行：
/plugin install security-guidance@claude-plugins-official

全プラン無料。入れない理由がない。
皆さんClaudeCodeにLet'sGO！

で、今日のアプデもそうだけど最近
「Claude Code進化早すぎて、正直ついていけてない…」
って感じてる人へ。
その感覚、あってます。
ここ最近だけでも、
・/simplify → /code-review
・Plugins
・権限管理まわり
・レビュー設計
・Hooks
・Subagents

とか、思想レベルでかなり変わってきてる。

ただ、この変化についていけるかで、
半年後の生産性かなり変わると思う。
なので、
「後で追えばいいや」より、
最低限だけでも今追った方がいい。
なので今回、先週のClaude Codeアップデート、
全部この下の記事で整理しました👇是非これで追いついてください。

content:
Hermes × Grokで
「毎朝自動投稿AIエージェント」を作ってみた🤖✨
やっていることはシンプル👇

1️⃣ Macのlaunchdで毎朝7:30に起動
2️⃣ Hermesが今日の日付・記念日テーマを取得
3️⃣ テーマに沿って画像生成プロンプトを作成
4️⃣ Grok ImagineでAI美女画像を3枚生成
5️⃣ そのうち1枚を動画化
6️⃣ Xに画像3枚を投稿
7️⃣ 動画をその投稿へのリプライとして投稿

ざっくり言うと、
🧠 Hermes
→ 考える・選ぶ・指示する・投稿する
🎨 Grok / Grok Imagine
→ 画像・動画を生成する
という役割分担。
つまり、Hermes × Grokを組み合わせると、
ただの画像生成ではなく、
✅ 毎日テーマを考える
✅ 画像を生成する
✅ 動画化する
✅ Xへ投稿する
ここまで自動で動く
“毎朝投稿AIエージェント” が作れる。

Mac向けの構成はこんな感じ👇

💻 Mac
🤖 Hermes Agent
🎨 Grok / Grok Imagine
📮 X投稿用CLI
⏰ launchdで定期実行
📁 画像・動画の保存フォルダ
📝 ログ管理
費用感はざっくり👇

💰 Hermes Agent本体
→ セルフホストなら無料
💻 Mac実行
→ 自前Macなら追加サーバー代なし

𝕏 X Premium
→ 日本Web価格で月918円〜

⚡ SuperGrok
→ 目安 $30/月
📮 その他（xAI APIなど）
→ Xへの1投稿2円〜

X Premium + SuperGrok があれば、
個人クリエイターでもかなり現実的に試せる構成。
これから個人クリエイターの運用は、
毎回手で作るよりも、
“自分専用のAIエージェントに
企画・生成・投稿まで任せる”
方向に寄っていくと思う。

Hermesが考え、
Grokが生成し、
Xへ届ける。
これ、かなり面白いよ🤖🔥

AIが生成した過去の誤情報を再び検索・参照しないよう、入力データを厳格に管理することが安定運用の鍵となります。

家帰ってきた瞬間、玄関にあるタイムロッキングコンテナにスマホを入れて、出る時にスマホ回収。つまり家ではスマホを一切触らない生活始めてから3日が経ちました...。
・

『ﾏｯｯｯｯｼﾞで人生変わってます!!!!!』
・

ちゃんとした精神科で検査はしてないんですがおそらくわたし、ADHD傾向高くて、スマホに使ってる時間は日本人平均より長いです。。

なので今まで、集中力上がる薬飲んでみたり、スマホを白黒カラーのみにしてみたり...

他にも色々対策試してみてたんですが
全部、ことごとく失敗してきた。

けど、このルーティーン導入してからほんと調子が良い。

そもそも仕事はPCでやる。
仕事の連絡はPCから返せる。
外ではPC開けない時多いのでスマホから返す。

↑正直、これさえできれば良いのでこのルーティーンがワークしてる。

スマホ依存脱却できそうで、本当に人生が変わってる。いつもより仕事量も増えて、質も上がってる実感あり。

しかもタイムリソースだけでなく、ずっとサボってた家の掃除や自炊もできるくらいマインドリソースも取り戻すことができている。AI覚えるよりまず自分の時間の使い方見直したほうが絶対いいわ。（当たり前w）

→ MCP servers
→ subagents

The real power comes from the ecosystem around it.

content:
This is insane 😳
“AI is replacing SDRs” is the wrong narrative.

What’s actually happening is way more interesting.

The best teams are replacing the busywork around outbound.

I tried Bond today for a funding-signal campaign and immediately understood why this space is moving so fast.

You don’t sit there building workflows, scraping databases, enriching leads manually, or stitching together 5 different tools anymore.

You just describe what you want.

Bond understands the ICP, asks the right contextual questions, finds companies showing real buying signals, verifies the contacts, and turns it into outreach-ready prospects within minutes.

What stood out to me wasn’t just the speed.

It was the quality of context.

Recently funded companies.
Relevant decision-makers.
Actual timing signals behind the outreach.

That’s a massive difference from the generic “spray and pray” outbound most people are still doing.

Honestly feels like GTM tools are entering their “ChatGPT moment.”

The interface is becoming conversation-first instead of workflow-first.

And once you experience that shift, traditional prospecting starts feeling painfully old.

content:
This is insane 🤯
This open-source tool gives AI instant knowledge of your entire codebase.

It’s called SocratiCode.

Instead of making AI randomly read files or run endless searches, it builds an index of the entire repository.

So the AI already knows:

• where features are implemented
• how modules connect
• which files depend on each other
• where specific logic exists

Even in million-line codebases.

Setup is surprisingly simple.

All you need is Docker running.

Then install the MCP server in your editor.

Works with:

• VS Code
• Cursor
• Claude Desktop
• Windsurf
• Cline
• Codex CLI

And the install command is literally just:

npx -y socraticode

After that you can ask your AI things like:

• “How authentication works in this project?”
• “Where is rate limiting implemented?”
• “What depends on this module?”

And it finds the answer across the entire repo.

Pretty wild what AI dev tools are becoming.

content:
Andrej Karpathy didn’t just share a CLAUDE.md file.

He accidentally revealed what software engineering is becoming.

The craziest part?

Most people still think AI coding is about writing smarter prompts.

Meanwhile the best engineers are building entire operating systems around agents.

That’s the real shift.

Karpathy’s workflow philosophy exposed something huge:

LLMs are not powerful because they’re intelligent.

They’re powerful because they can follow systems relentlessly.

And once developers realized that…

everything changed.

That’s why CLAUDE.md files suddenly became a thing across the industry.

Not as prompts.

As behavioral infrastructure.

A way to force discipline onto stochastic models.

Because left alone, AI agents do the same things junior engineers do:

- overengineer simple tasks
- pretend they understand
- rewrite things nobody asked for
- optimize for looking done
- fail silently

So the smartest developers stopped “prompting.”

Instead, they started building environments.

Rules.
Constraints.
Verification loops.
Execution frameworks.

Basically:

turning AI into managed engineering labor.

And now people are running multiple Claude Code agents in parallel like an actual software org:

• one mapping the codebase
• one writing tests
• one debugging failures
• one reviewing diffs
• one researching solutions
• one validating outputs

Not AI assistance.

Agent orchestration.

Karpathy hinted at the most important shift with one idea:

Stop telling the model exactly what to do.

Instead:
define success conditions and let it iterate until it reaches them.

That sounds small.

It’s not.

Because the engineer’s role fundamentally changes.

The bottleneck is no longer:
“who can code the fastest?”

It becomes:

“who can design the best cognitive system around AI agents?”

That’s why this feels different from every AI hype cycle before it.

The leverage is real now.

A single engineer with well-structured agents can suddenly operate with the output of an entire team.

And honestly?

I think most people are still underestimating how massive this shift is about to become.

content:
Someone is going to build the first AI that knows more about your life than your coworkers do.

This repo feels dangerously close to that future.

OpenHuman is an open-source “personal AI operating system” that continuously builds long-term memory about you from:

• emails
• Slack chats
• GitHub repos
• calendars
• docs
• notes
• meetings
• workflows

Then compresses everything into a persistent Memory Tree stored locally on your machine.

Not just chat history.

Actual evolving context.

And honestly, this is the part that caught my attention:

Most AI assistants still forget everything the second the conversation ends.

OpenHuman doesn’t.

It keeps syncing your digital life every 20 minutes and turns it into an Obsidian-style knowledge vault your AI can continuously learn from.

That changes everything.

Because the real moat in AI probably won’t be “who has the smartest model.”

It’ll be:

“Which AI understands you best?”

The repo also packs:

• 118+ integrations
• built-in model routing
• local-first memory
• voice conversations
• browser + scraper tools
• coding agents
• Gmail/Slack/GitHub access
• autonomous background syncing

And unlike most “AI agent” projects…

this one actually feels designed for normal humans, not just terminal power users.

Feels less like a chatbot…

…and more like the early prototype of a real personal AI companion.

100% open source
